Picking up from where I left off: the heart is really two pumps side by side. Blood that has given up its oxygen comes back from the body through the two biggest veins, the superior and inferior vena cava, and flows into the right atrium [1]. From there it goes into the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs. In the lungs it drops off carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen. The oxygen-rich blood then returns to the left atrium, passes into the left ventricle, and gets pumped out through the aorta to the rest of the body [2].

Four valves keep the blood moving in one direction only. The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle, the pulmonary valve between the right ventricle and the lungs, the mitral valve between the left atrium and left ventricle, and the aortic valve between the left ventricle and the aorta [1][2]. The heart's own electrical system sets the rhythm. A small cluster of cells in the right atrium, called the sinoatrial (SA) node, acts as a natural pacemaker. Its signal spreads across the atria and makes them squeeze blood down into the ventricles. The signal then passes through the atrioventricular (AV) node to the ventricles, which contract to push blood out [3]. The SA node usually fires at a steady pace, but it speeds up or slows down depending on whether you're active or resting and on your emotions [1].
